title: The problem of induction
examples: What is the difference between induction and deduction?
How did Hume challenge our everyday thinking?
Can science ever be 100 percent certain?

explain.say: Today we explore the problem of induction in thinking.

items: Conclusion: The sun will rise tomorrow

explain.say: Induction is moving from specific past observations to general future rules.
Consider the black swan, an example that challenges our assumptions.
David Hume questioned if past experience truly guarantees future results.
Karl Popper suggested science should use falsification, not just confirmation.
In everyday life, we use induction when planning our daily routines.

faq.q: Does this mean science cannot make any predictions?
faq.a: No, it means predictions are always provisional, not absolute proof. You might also ask: Are scientific laws certain? Or: Can science ever be wrong?

faq.q: What is the difference between induction and deduction?
faq.a: Deduction starts with general rules to reach a specific conclusion. Induction goes from many specific observations to a general rule. You could also ask: Which is more certain?
asks: General to specific vs. specific to general

faq.q: Why is the black swan so important to this topic?
faq.a: It represents an event that contradicts all previous observations. It shows that our past data is not a perfect guide for the future. You might also ask: What does the black swan teach us?
asks: What is an outlier in science?

faq.q: What exactly does Popper mean by falsification?
faq.a: It means that a theory must be capable of being proven false by evidence. If no evidence can ever disprove it, it is not scientific. You could also ask: How do I test a theory properly?

faq.q: Did Hume suggest that we should stop making predictions?
faq.a: No, he suggested we should be very careful about how we claim certainty. He argued that our belief in cause and effect is a habit, not pure logic. You might also ask: Is our belief in cause natural?

facts: Induction moves from specific instances to general theories.
Hume argued that our belief in cause is based on habit, not pure reason.
Popper proposed that scientific theories must be falsifiable to be scientific.
A black swan is a real-world example of an unexpected observation.

quiz.say: If every swan you see is white, what does induction suggest about the next swan?
quiz.show: Prediction: The next swan is white.

options.show: The next swan will be white, but only if we test it.
options.say: The next swan will be white, but only if we test it.

options.show: The next swan is likely white.
options.say: The next swan is likely white.

options.show: The next swan must be black.
options.say: The next swan must be black.

options.show: We cannot say anything about the next swan.
options.say: We cannot say anything about the next swan.

quiz.why: Induction predicts the next swan will be white because all previous swans were white.

wrong.0: This confuses testing with prediction; induction makes a prediction first.
wrong.2: This is too extreme; it ignores all the evidence you have seen.
wrong.3: This is too cautious; it ignores the pattern you have observed.

quiz.say: What was Hume's main philosophical challenge to science?

options.show: Science cannot make any predictions at all.
options.say: Science cannot make any predictions at all.

options.show: We must use deduction only in science.
options.say: We must use deduction only in science.

options.show: We must only look at the black swans.
options.say: We must only look at the black swans.

options.show: Our belief in cause is based on habit, not pure logic.
options.say: Our belief in cause is based on habit, not pure logic.

quiz.why: Hume argued that we assume cause and effect simply because it has always happened together.

wrong.0: This is too strong; Hume questioned certainty, not possibility.
wrong.1: This ignores the actual process of building scientific knowledge.
wrong.2: This ignores the vast body of evidence supporting the general rule.

quiz.say: According to Popper, what must a scientific theory possess?

options.show: It must be possible to prove the theory wrong.
options.say: It must be possible to prove the theory wrong.

options.show: It must be proven true by all evidence.
options.say: It must be proven true by all evidence.

options.show: It must only use deductive logic.
options.say: It must only use deductive logic.

options.show: It must explain every possible outcome.
options.say: It must explain every possible outcome.

quiz.why: Falsifiability means there must be some conceivable observation that could disprove the idea.

wrong.1: This is impossible; no amount of evidence can prove something absolutely true.
wrong.2: Popper was concerned with how theories are tested, not just the logic used.
wrong.3: A theory that explains everything often explains nothing useful.
